date.note: Section 11 of the 1936 paper; corrections published 1937.

explanation: Turing states that the results of §8 show the Hilbert Entscheidungsproblem can have no solution. He refers to Hilbert and Ackermann for the formulation and proposes to show there can be no general process for determining whether a given formula U of the functional calculus Z is provable. He distinguishes this from Gödel's results: Gödel showed there are propositions U such that neither U nor its negation is provable, whereas Turing shows there is no general method telling whether a given U is provable, equivalently whether Z with the negation of U adjoined is consistent. For each computing machine M he constructs a formula Un(M) whose interpretation is that 0 appears in some complete configuration of M. Lemma 1 shows that if 0 appears then Un(M) is provable; Lemma 2 shows that if Un(M) is provable then 0 appears. Hence a general provability decision process would decide whether M ever prints 0, which §8 shows impossible. Therefore the Entscheidungsproblem cannot be solved.

The paper notes that the proof contained formal errors, corrected in the 1937 correction, where a new functional variable G is introduced and the formula Un(M) is modified

explanation: Turing first puts each machine table into a standard form in which every operation is one of a small set of forms such as erase-and-move or print-and-move. He numbers the m-configurations q1,...,qR and the symbols S0,S1,...,Sm, with blank as S0, 0 as S1, and 1 as S2. Each line becomes an expression like qi Sj Sk L qm, and all such expressions separated by semicolons form the standard description (S.D). Replacing qi by D followed by i copies of A, and Sj by D followed by j copies of C, and finally substituting digits for A, C, D, L, R, N, and semicolon yields an arabic numeral, the description number (D.N). The D.N determines the S.D and the machine uniquely; each computable sequence corresponds to at least one D.N, and no D.N corresponds to more than one computable sequence. Hence the computable sequences are enumerable. This encoding is what makes the universal machine and the diagonal argument possible.

The encoding is a technical device, not a claim about the nature of computation
problem: To apply diagonal arguments and to build a universal machine, Turing needs a uniform finite encoding of arbitrary machine tables that can be written on a tape and manipulated mechanically.

explanation: Turing says the computable numbers include the real parts of all algebraic numbers, the real parts of the zeros of Bessel functions, and numbers such as π and e. He also says the computable numbers do not include all definable numbers and gives an example of a definable number which is not computable. Although the class is great and in many ways similar to the reals, it is nevertheless enumerable. The enumeration follows from the description-number encoding: each computable sequence corresponds to at least one description number, and no description number corresponds to more than one computable sequence. The non-computable definable number is the sequence P whose n-th figure is 1 or 0 according as n is or is not satisfactory; by the theorem of §8, P is not computable. Turing notes it may be possible to calculate any assigned number of figures of P, but not by a uniform process; when sufficiently many figures have been calculated, an essentially new method is necessary for more.

date.note: Published in Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society, Series 2, Vol. 43 (1937), pages 544-546.

explanation: In the 1937 correction, Turing states that his proof of the insolubility of the Entscheidungsproblem contained some formal errors, and that other statements should be modified although not actually false as they stand. The expression for Inst{qi Sj Sk Lqo} is corrected, and the statement that Inst{qa Sb Sd Lqc} & F[n+1] implies CCn → CCn+1 is declared false even with the new expression, because one cannot deduce F[n+1] → (¬F(u,u'')) and therefore cannot use the term involving F(y',z) in Inst. To correct this, Turing introduces a new functional variable G, with G(x,y) interpreted as 'x precedes y', and defines Q as an abbreviation for a formula expressing the needed ordering properties. The corrected Un(M) is then (∃u)A(M) → (∃s)(∃t)RS1(s,t), where A(M) includes Q. With these modifications the proof is correct, and Un(M) can be put in the prenex form with n = 4. Turing acknowledges P. Bernays for pointing out the errors.
